title: September 11, 2001
objective: After this level you can describe the attacks of September 11, 2001, and explain why historians treat very recent events differently from the distant past.
summary: On September 11, 2001, al-Qaeda hijackers killed 2,977 people. Recent history is harder to judge: records open slowly and verdicts take time.

cards.headline: On one morning in 2001, the United States was attacked at home.
cards.body: It is the most recent event in this tree. Studying it takes the same tools as any other, plus patience.

cards.headline: What happened
cards.body: On the morning of September 11, 2001, 19 terrorists from al-Qaeda, an Islamist extremist group, hijacked four commercial airplanes. They crashed two into the North and South Towers of the World Trade Center in New York, and a third into the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia.

cards.headline: Flight 93 and the toll
cards.body: On the fourth plane, Flight 93, passengers learned of the other attacks and fought back. The plane crashed into a field in western Pennsylvania. The attacks killed 2,977 people: 2,753 in New York, 184 at the Pentagon and 40 on Flight 93.

cards.headline: Why recent history is harder
cards.body: Historians of the distant past can read records that were once closed. For recent events, many records are still locked. Under the Presidential Records Act, the public can request a president’s records only five years after the administration ends, and some may be restricted for up to 12 years. The primary sources that explain big decisions arrive slowly.

cards.headline: Give it time
cards.body: Remember Level 64? Matthew Josephson judged the Gilded Age giants in 1934, and Allan Nevins answered him in 1940. Historians can already state what happened on September 11. Why it happened and what it changed will be argued for a long time, as the records open.

cards.headline: September 11, 2001: explained
learned: 19 al-Qaeda terrorists hijacked four planes on 9/11
Flight 93’s passengers fought back; 2,977 people were killed
Records of recent events open slowly
Verdicts on recent history take time

questions.prompt: Match each place with how many people the attacks killed there.
questions.explanation: The attacks killed 2,977 people: 2,753 in New York, 184 at the Pentagon and 40 on Flight 93.

questions.prompt: A historian wants records from a presidency that ended three years ago. What does the Presidential Records Act mean for her?

options.label: She can read all of them today
options.rationale: Public requests open only after five years.

options.label: She must wait: public requests open five years after the administration ends
The records are destroyed after 12 years
options.rationale: Twelve years is the limit on some restrictions, not destruction.

options.label: Only foreign governments may request them
options.rationale: The act gives the US public a path to request them.

questions.explanation: The public can request a president’s records five years after the administration ends, and some may stay restricted for up to 12 years.

questions.prompt: Josephson and Nevins published their verdicts on the Gilded Age decades after the events. What does that suggest about judging September 11?

options.label: The first account written is always the final one
options.rationale: Josephson’s verdict was answered by Nevins six years later.

options.label: Recent events cannot be studied at all
options.rationale: Historians can already state what happened.

options.label: Only eyewitnesses may write its history
options.rationale: Historians study events they did not witness.

options.label: Verdicts on why and what it changed will take time and more records

questions.explanation: What happened is known; interpretations of why and what changed will develop as records open and time passes.
